summary: we developed an interactive application and a dedicated companion website (a "story archive") backed by in-depth research. Our platform highlights three specific spacecraft intentionally left behind on the Moon and Mars after completing their missions. Since the 1960s, NASA has left hardware across the solar system, yet most people never hear the full story behind them. Our project bridges this gap by presenting each spacecraft's original mission, the timeline and reasons for its abandonment, its current resting location, and engineering concepts for how we could potentially retrieve and bring them back to Earth. To a casual viewer, abandoned space hardware might just look like space debris, but these machines represent the first chapters of humanity's presence on other worlds. Preserving their stories honors the scientific breakthroughs they achieved, educates the public on the history of space exploration, and inspires future solutions for sustainable space travel and hardware retrieval.

projectRefs: NASA Data & Space Agency Resources Used (edit if anything here isn’t true for your team):  We used public NASA and space-agency information to write the story of each object. NASA JPL’s report on the GRAIL impact site and NASA Science’s Mars Global Surveyor page gave us dates, locations and mission results. NASA’s MAVEN coverage and Hasselblad’s history of its Moon cameras confirmed how those missions ended. We used the NASA Open Data Portal (data.nasa.gov) and the Planetary Data System to identify datasets we plan to link from each story page, such as GRAIL gravity data and Mars Global Surveyor images. In the prototype, we summarized these facts into short story cards, and we used the Space Apps challenge image of the Mars rover family.

References & External Resources:  Code: our own HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, with no external libraries. Fonts: Bricolage Grotesque, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono (Google Fonts, SIL Open Font License). Images: the Mars rover photo from the NASA Space Apps challenge page; the spacecraft illustrations were drawn by our team. Data and facts: NASA JPL, NASA Science, PBS NewsHour, Hasselblad, the NASA Open Data Portal (data.nasa.gov) and the NASA Planetary Data System. Tools: the site was built with help from Claude, an AI assistant by Anthropic.
